strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: improving fine-grained semantic alignment and 3D spatial/geometric consistency in text-to-3D generation across both optimization-based and feed-forward paradigms.
Proposes a simple, general plug-and-play idea: repurposing a VLM as a differentiable critic via Yes/No log-odds over multi-view renderings.

Demonstrates qualitative improvements on several challenging prompts, including the 'Embracing Peace' statue, sailor, glove, glass window, and backpack examples, where baselines show semantic omissions or spatial failures.
Reports quantitative gains on GPTEval3D for the optimization-based setting and on CLIP-D/FID/CLIP-FID/Geo for the feed-forward setting, suggesting the reward signal may be useful.
Includes ablations on the geometric query and multi-view input, and provides an honest limitations section discussing struggles with long or highly detailed prompts.
weaknesses: The central differentiability claim is under-specified. The paper states that theta -> rendered images -> r_VLM is differentiable and that gradients can be backpropagated through Qwen2.5-VL 7B, but it provides no details on how gradients flow through the VLM's vision encoder and LLM to multi-view rendered images, memory/compute cost, gradient checkpointing, precision, how many VLM evaluations are used per optimization step, or whether the Yes/No logits are calibrated enough to serve as a meaningful reward.

The 'dual-query' design is effectively a single conjunctive Yes/No query. A single scalar reward conflates semantic and geometric failures, so the method does not actually provide separate semantic and spatial critics despite the framing. There is no validation that r_VLM correlates with human judgments, that the VLM attends to all views, or that it is not reward-hacked by the optimization.

The optimization-based evaluation in Table 1 is not sufficiently justified. It is unclear whether all baselines were rerun under the same GPT-4o-mini pairwise protocol or whether some Elo numbers were copied from the original GPTEval3D benchmark. No error bars, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported. The dynamic lambda_VLM schedule, number of SDS steps, rendering resolution, and other hyperparameters are omitted.

The feed-forward evaluation in Table 2 is very weak. It appears to evaluate FID, CLIP-FID, and an undefined Geometry score on only the few cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4, which is far too small for FID-style metrics. The Geometry metric is not defined, the number of samples is not stated, and no human evaluation or simple guidance baseline is provided.

The test-time guidance equation (Eq. 10) is unprincipled as written. Adding the gradient of r_VLM with respect to z_t directly to the sampler output, without derivation or scaling by the denoising process, is not obviously a valid posterior-sampling update. The paper provides no theoretical justification or ablation for lambda_TTG or the guidance schedule.

Ablation studies are qualitative only. The geometry-query and multi-view ablations show images but no metrics, and there is no ablation on the semantic query, reward scale, VLM choice, number of views, or whether backpropagating through the VLM is necessary versus using it as a non-differentiable filter/reward.

Reproducibility is poor. No code, evaluation scripts, model versions/checkpoints, full prompt sets, or detailed compute measurements are provided. The claim of 60 seconds per feed-forward asset with VLM guidance at every one of 50 sampling steps is not substantiated.

Novelty and related work are not adequately positioned. Prior work on VLM feedback/reward for text-to-3D generation (e.g., DreamSync-style refinement or other VLM-guided 3D methods) is not discussed, and the 'first attempt' claim is not convincingly supported. The comparison to existing VLM/preference-based rewards is limited to DreamReward and DreamDPO.

Presentation has several issues: Table 1 includes methods not listed in the setup, Table 2 metric directions and definitions are unclear, some figure captions and references have formatting/typo problems, and key implementation details are absent.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important problem: text-to-3D generators (both SDS-based and feed-forward/native-3D) do suffer from weak semantic grounding and poor spatial/part-assembly reasoning, and injecting stronger, language-grounded priors is a reasonable research direction.

The generality claim is at least demonstrated across two paradigms — a reward for SDS-style optimization (Eq. 9) and test-time guidance on a native 3D DiT sampler (Eq. 10) — which is a broader scope than most single-paradigm papers.

Some qualitative results are visually striking (e.g., the 'Embracing Peace' statue in Fig. 1), and the paper includes a limitations discussion that honestly acknowledges the failure to capture fine details like the nurse's lifted leg, as well as a sensitivity/perturbation study (Fig. 5).
The method is conceptually simple and could be cheaply integrated as a plug-in critic, which is a practical advantage if the underlying claims hold.
weaknesses: The central technical claim — a 'fully differentiable' VLM reward via Yes/No log-odds — is asserted but not substantiated. Backpropagating the log-odds of discrete 'Yes'/'No' tokens through a 7B VLM down to rendered pixel values is notoriously noisy and prone to reward hacking. There is no analysis of gradient quality, no variance study, and no discussion of the well-known failure mode where LLM/VLM-based differentiable rewards are exploited by the optimizer rather than genuinely improving semantics.

The core 'dual-query' contribution is essentially a single prompt template containing two criteria (Sec. 4.2). Calling this a novel 'dual-query critic signal' overstates the mechanism; the Yes/No log-odds reward formulation closely mirrors prior VLM-as-reward work (e.g., Rocamonde et al. 'VLM are zero-shot reward models', ImageReward-style log-odds rewards), and classifier-style guidance (Eq. 10) is a long-established idea. The novelty is therefore modest and insufficiently differentiated from existing literature; the related-work section does not engage with VLM-as-reward for 3D or for generative guidance at all.

The quantitative evaluation is weak and in places not credible. Table 1 reports Elo scores on GPTEval3D but gives no confidence intervals, no statistical significance, and no seed/variance information, despite the improvements being within noise for several metrics. Worse, the evaluation is performed by GPT-4o-mini — itself a VLM — which risks circularity/self-serving bias when the method being evaluated is explicitly optimized with a VLM critic.

Table 2 is problematic: the 'Geometry' metric is never defined, CLIP-FID is redundant with CLIP-D/FID, and the quantitative numbers are computed on 'all cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4' — i.e., roughly a dozen examples. Reporting FID and CLIP-FID on ~10 samples is statistically meaningless, so the claimed 'significant improvements across the board' are unsupported.

Ablations are entirely qualitative (Fig. 6, Fig. 5). There is no quantitative ablation of the geometry query, of multi-view vs. single-view inputs, or of the key hyperparameter λ_VLM and its annealing schedule, even though λ is described as critical to the method's success.

Reproducibility is inadequate: critical implementation details (annealing schedule, λ values, λ_TTG, number of views, rendering resolution, VLM checkpoint/tokenization of 'Yes'/'No') are deferred to a supplementary that is not available, and no code is provided. The feed-forward results are run only on a single A100 and evaluated on a handful of prompts.

The paper overclaims: 'to the best of our knowledge, VLM3D makes the first attempt to establish a principled and generalizable path to inject the VLM's understanding into 3D pipelines.' This is not defensible given prior VLM-guided/reward-based 3D and VLM-reward literature, and the related-work section omits it.

Demonstrations rely on cherry-picked, unusually long prompts (Fig. 1) to expose baseline failures, which inflates the apparent improvement. No systematic study of prompt length/complexity is provided, despite this being the acknowledged failure mode.

Some qualitative 'corrections' are unconvincing on inspection (e.g., the 'leather glove' in Fig. 4 resembles a mitten rather than a corrected glove), undermining the claim that the critic reliably fixes part assembly rather than merely shifting the failure mode.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem—improving both semantic fidelity and spatial coherence in text-to-3D generation—and does so in a way that spans two distinct paradigms (optimization-based SDS and native 3D feed-forward sampling).

The core idea of extracting a differentiable critic from a VLM's Yes/No log-odds (Eq. 8) is simple and cleanly formulated, and the dual-query prompt that jointly checks 'Content Match' and 'Geometric Quality' is a sensible design that is at least partially validated by the ablation in Fig. 6.

The optimization-based results on the 110-prompt GPTEval3D benchmark are strong: VLM3D leads on all six metrics (Table 1), and the qualitative comparisons (Fig. 1, 3, 5) convincingly show recovery of fine-grained semantics (e.g., 'kaleidoscope,' multi-instrument scenes) where DreamReward/DreamDPO miss details.

Applying the same reward as test-time guidance inside the DiT sampling loop of a frozen feed-forward model (Eq. 10) is a practical contribution that requires no retraining, and the qualitative correction of severe part-assembly failures (Fig. 1, 4) is compelling.

The paper is generally well written, the framework figure is clear, and the limitations section (Sec. 6) honestly acknowledges that long/detailed prompts are not fully captured and that the reward does not yet exploit the VLM's full reasoning.
Ablations on the geometric query and on multi-view vs. single-view input (Fig. 6) provide useful mechanistic evidence that both components matter.
weaknesses: The feed-forward evaluation is very weakly supported. Table 2 reports CLIP-D, FID, CLIP-FID, and an undefined 'Geo.' score, but the setup states the evaluation is over 'all cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4'—i.e., a handful of prompts. No sample size, no error bars, and no significance testing are given, so the reported improvements cannot be considered reliable.

The 'Geometry' metric in Table 2 is never defined, and the directionality of several metrics (CLIP-D is marked ↓, which is unusual) is not explained. This undermines reproducibility of the feed-forward claims.

The test-time guidance in Eq. 10 is methodologically underspecified. It is unclear how the VLM reward is computed from a *noisy* latent z_t at each of 50 steps (e.g., via an x0-prediction, a clean render, etc.), how gradients are backpropagated through a 7B VLM plus a differentiable renderer at every step, and whether the claimed 60 s/asset is compatible with that cost. This is a substantial reproducibility gap for the second paradigm.

Novelty is moderate. Using a reward/VLM signal to augment SDS is closely related to DreamReward and related preference-reward works; the distinctive element (the dual-query Yes/No log-odds) is largely prompt engineering rather than a new mechanism. The 'first attempt' claim and the generality framing are somewhat overstated given this prior art.

Fairness of the feed-forward comparison is questionable: guidance is applied only to Hunyuan3D, while CLAY and Hunyuan3D are treated as unguided baselines. A controlled comparison (same backbone with and without guidance) and a VLM-reward-only baseline would be more informative.

Important implementation details are missing or deferred entirely to the supplement: the number of rendered views N, the exact λ_VLM annealing schedule, the balancing of L_SDS and r_VLM, and the rendering/gradient pathway. For a method paper this is a meaningful omission.

In the optimization paradigm, the Elo numbers in Table 1 appear to be taken from the GPTEval3D benchmark for the baselines, with no variance or confidence intervals reported for the VLM3D row; the size of the reported margin is therefore hard to assess statistically.

There is a possible evaluation circularity/leakage concern: the reward model is a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) and the benchmark evaluator is also a VLM (GPT-4o-mini), so gains on 'alignment' metrics may partially reflect VLM-to-VLM agreement rather than human-perceived fidelity.

strengths: Proposes a general and novel framework for using VLM Yes/No log-odds as a differentiable semantic and spatial critic, applicable to both optimization-based (SDS) and native 3D feed-forward generation.

Dual-query prompt design explicitly couples content match and geometric quality; ablations show removing the geometry query or using single-view input reintroduces Janus artifacts, floating parts, and fractured surfaces.

Strong qualitative demonstrations of correcting severe failures, e.g., recovering both figures in the Embracing Peace statue and repairing the disconnected Navy sailor parts, where MVDream/Hunyuan3D fail.
Integrates the critic into two distinct pipelines with concrete pseudo-code, hyperparameter schedules, and an engineering fix for differentiable VLM image preprocessing.
Includes multiple ablation studies (prompt design, guidance scheduling, VLM-only vs SDS-only, external 3D-native metrics) that support design choices and show complementary benefits.
Honest limitations section acknowledges that long/detailed prompts remain challenging and that the VLM reward does not fully exploit the VLM's visual reasoning.
weaknesses: Optimization benchmark comparison may be invalid: Appendix A.3 states some baseline results are taken from threestudio/GPTEval3D rather than uniformly rerun, while VLM3D is evaluated with GPT-4o-mini; mixing judges (GPT-4V vs GPT-4o-mini) and sources undermines the Elo comparisons in Table 1.
Table 1 reports Elo scores without confidence intervals or significance tests; the claim of significant outperformance is not statistically supported.

Feed-forward quantitative evaluation is weak: only 24 prompts, FID/CLIP-FID are unreliable at this sample size, and the Geometry Score is not defined in the main paper; the appendix does not clearly specify the reference meshes or ground truth used for Chamfer/Hausdorff distances, making Table 2 hard to interpret or reproduce.

The VLM critic itself is not independently validated: there is no study showing that Yes/No log-odds correlate with human judgments of semantics or geometry, and using softmax over only two token logits ignores all other tokens, making the reward uncalibrated and vulnerable to reward hacking.

The core technical contribution—making the VLM image preprocessor fully differentiable—is described mainly in the appendix and not in sufficient detail in the main text; gradient quality, stability, and failure modes are not analyzed.

The dual-query design conflates semantic and geometric criteria into a single scalar; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation and defers disentanglement to future work, so it cannot diagnose which criterion fails.

Test-time guidance is demonstrated only on Hunyuan3D and requires expensive per-step decoding/rendering plus VLM backpropagation (60s added runtime, 53GB memory); scalability and transfer to other feed-forward models are not established.
Presentation is sloppy, with typos ('VM3D'), garbled figure captions, inconsistent model versions (Hunyuan3D 2.0 vs 2.1), and missing code URL, which hinders clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: semantic and spatial fidelity in text-to-3D generation remains a major challenge, and leveraging VLMs as critics is a promising direction.
The core idea of using the log-odds of a binary Yes/No VLM response as a differentiable reward signal is clean, general, and potentially applicable across different 3D generation paradigms.
Demonstrates the framework on both optimization-based (SDS) and feed-forward (test-time guidance) pipelines, showing versatility.
The technical contribution of making the VLM's image preprocessor fully differentiable is non-trivial and practically useful for gradient-based reward optimization.
Ablation studies on prompt design, guidance scheduling, and multi-view vs. single-view input provide some insight into the method's behavior.
The paper is generally well-organized and the method is described with sufficient clarity for an expert reader to understand the approach.
weaknesses: The quantitative evidence is weak and does not convincingly support the central claims. The improvements in Table 1 (GPTEval3D Elo scores) are marginal, and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported. The evaluation set (110 prompts) is modest for drawing strong conclusions.

Table 2 contains suspicious values: CLIP-D scores of 0.19–0.23 are far outside the typical range for CLIP cosine similarity (often 0.6–0.9). This raises concerns about the metric's correctness or the evaluation protocol, undermining confidence in the reported feed-forward improvements.

The feed-forward evaluation is extremely limited: only 24 prompts, and the comparison is only against two baselines (CLAY and Hunyuan3D). This is insufficient to support broad claims about correcting spatial and semantic failures.

The custom 'Geometry Score' in Table 2 is not a standard metric and is defined only in the appendix. Its lack of validation makes the reported improvements difficult to interpret or compare with prior work.

The ablation study (Section 5.3) is largely qualitative and incomplete. The tables in Appendix C (Tables 4–7) report proxy metrics (gradient norm, VLM reward, CLIP score) rather than downstream generation quality metrics (e.g., FID, CLIP-FID, GPTEval3D), leaving the impact of design choices on final 3D quality unclear.

The paper does not compare against other VLM-based reward methods (e.g., VLM-RM, ImageReward), making it impossible to assess whether the specific log-odds formulation is superior to simpler alternatives.

Reproducibility is limited: the code is referenced but not available in the submitted manuscript. The key modification to the VLM preprocessor is described only briefly in the appendix, and the baseline CLAY is evaluated using a non-public demo, raising reproducibility concerns.

The evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o-mini for pairwise comparisons in GPTEval3D, but potential biases of the LLM evaluator are not analyzed or controlled for. This is a common issue, but the paper does not address it.

The limitations section acknowledges that the method still misses fine details (e.g., the Embracing Peace statue's lifted leg), but the main text and abstract make stronger claims about 'precise prompt alignment' and 'high-fidelity textures and geometry' that are not fully supported by the evidence.

strengths: The framework is genuinely general: the same r_VLM = z_yes - z_no critic is demonstrated both as a reward objective for SDS optimization and as a test-time guidance module for native 3D feed-forward samplers (Hunyuan3D), showing applicability across two distinct paradigms.

The dual-criteria query design (Content Match + Geometric Quality) is a sensible and well-motivated response to the two documented failure modes (coarse semantics and poor spatial coherence) of existing methods.

The re-engineering of the VLM image preprocessor to use Torch tensors instead of NumPy (Appendix A.1) is a real and non-trivial technical contribution that enables end-to-end gradient flow, which is a prerequisite for the method.

Evidence is multi-pronged and largely consistent: Table 1 (GPTEval3D Elo), Table 2 (CLIP-D/FID/Geo for feed-forward), and the external 3D-native metrics in Table 6 (ULIP, Uni3D) all favor the method, which partially mitigates concerns about VLM-based judging.
The ablation suite is useful, covering prompt design, guidance scheduling (Table 5), single-view vs. multi-view inputs, geometry-query removal (Fig. 7), and a VLM-only baseline (Table 7).

The limitations section is honest, explicitly acknowledging that fine-grained details (e.g., the nurse's lifted leg in the Embracing Peace example) are still missed and that the reward does not fully exploit the VLM's reasoning.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: using a VLM as a reward/critic is well established in the image and 3D literature; the novel elements are the specific dual-criteria query and the differentiable preprocessor, both of which are engineering-level rather than conceptual advances.

Circular evaluation in the prompt ablation: Table 4 selects the prompt design by comparing the VLM's own reward, which is exactly the quantity being optimized, so it cannot independently establish that the dual-query prompt is better; downstream (e.g., CLIP/Elo) evaluation is needed here.

Potential evaluator-method correlation: the method optimizes against Qwen2.5-VL while GPTEval3D judging uses GPT-4o-mini, so a VLM-judged benchmark may systematically favor VLM-optimized outputs; this bias is not controlled or discussed.

Evaluation scale is small for the feed-forward claim: Table 2 uses only 24 prompts, and no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any quantitative result, making it hard to judge whether the modest margins (e.g., Table 1 alignment 1365.5 vs. 1298.9) are reliable.

Several metrics are under-specified: 'FID' and 'CLIP-FID' for 3D assets are not defined (on what distribution of renderings?), and the self-defined 'Geometry Score' is only described in an appendix, making the feed-forward comparison difficult to interpret.
The 'dual-query' terminology is misleading — the method actually issues a single query containing two criteria, which matters for how the contribution is framed.

Resource requirements are high (49 GB optimization / 53 GB feed-forward memory) and depend on a re-engineered preprocessor; combined with the missing code URL ('Code is available at' with no link), reproducibility is constrained.
The geometric-quality criterion is evaluated qualitatively in Fig. 7 without a corresponding quantitative ablation, weakening the claim that the explicit geometry query is 'critical'.
